slides.title: Personal-agent identity
slides.subtitle: Verify agent metadata and same-domain signing keys before trusting assertions
slides.notes: A company needs a stable way to know which software is acting for a user. This example shows how it verifies a personal agent's public identity before it accepts anything the agent signs.

slides.title: The identity is a URL
slides.statement: The agent's HTTPS `client_id` points to **public metadata**: its name, redirect URIs and JWKS location.
slides.notes: There is no registration step. The client_id is itself an HTTPS URL, and what it serves describes the agent: its name, where users may be sent back to (HTTPS URLs on its own domain, or a loopback redirect URI for an app on the user's computer), and where its public signing keys live.

slides.title: Who takes part
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR M["Model"] subgraph CO["Company"] C["Company API
receives assertions"] end subgraph HOST["Your host, trusted"] direction TB H["PAP host"] -- "approve destination" --> R["Reactor
discovery policy"] end subgraph AD["Agent's domain, public"] direction LR I["agent.json
name, redirects, jwks_uri"] -- "points to" --> K["JWKS
public keys only"] end CO -- "resolve client_id" --> HOST HOST -- "GET, no credentials" --> AD HOST -- "verified identity" --> CO HOST -. "identity and policy only" .-> M
slides.caption: Only public documents cross; the private key stays with its custodian and never appears here.
slides.notes: Begin at the company, which wants to know who signs the assertions it receives, so it asks for the client_id URL to be resolved. Inside the host, every fetch is first approved by the Reactor discovery policy. The host then reads the agent's domain without credentials: agent.json, which points to the JWKS holding only public keys. The verified identity goes back to the company. The model, off to the side, sees the identity and its signing policy, never the key coordinates or raw metadata.

slides.title: How it flows
slides.notes: The destination is approved, the metadata fetched without credentials, and its schema checked. The identity it declares must be exactly the URL that was requested. The JWKS must live on the allowed domain, and only then are the public keys fetched.

slides.title: Trust, or refuse
slides.caption: Each check closes a door; redirect URIs are read from the document, never inferred from a callback.
slides.notes: Read the checks left to right. The metadata must match the schema. The identity it declares must be exactly the URL that was requested, so a document cannot claim to be a different agent. Its JWKS must live on the allowed domain, so it cannot quietly hand its trust to keys hosted somewhere unrelated. Any no ends in a refusal. Only after all three are the public keys fetched and the identity verified. The redirect URIs come from the document too, explicit, never inferred from an incoming callback.

slides.title: What the model sees
slides.notes: The tool output describes policy: who the agent is and how its keys are governed. The key coordinates and the raw documents stay outside model context.

slides.title: Run it yourself
slides.cta: The Pydantic AI and Agent Runtimes examples verify an identity through AgentIdentityClient
slides.notes: Run either example to watch the checks pass. Then continue with Delegation, how a key from the agent's jwks_uri vouches for the key that signs its requests, and read the personal-agent guide.
